Recap
Here's a summary of today's key moments:
• Democrats are continuing to notch up wins in the US House of Representatives, extending their majority in the chamber.
• Two US Senate seats remain in doubt, with counting continuing in Alaska and Mississippi.
• As the dust settles, Republicans are searching for answers. Key figures say the Iran war and high petrol prices are a key factor.
• Democrats are discussing how they can best wield power in Congress, with universal healthcare, immigration and White House investigations on the agenda.

Hegseth backs Trump and Defense Department work after midterm losses
Donald Trump's Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has emerged for the first time since this week's Republican midterm losses.
Facing criticism of his role in the Trump administration's war in Iran, it appears that Hegseth is digging in.

"Ever since I walked up these very steps nearly two years ago, President Trump's War Department has never been afraid to lead the way," he says in a video posted on X today showing him outside his office.
"Just like the president, we don't back down and that especially applies now.
"The next few months and years are critical for our department and our republic.
"This is about the president's America First agenda. This is about our department's Peace Through Strength agenda."
If you'd like to watch his entire address, you can here:
Democrats could block future Trump Supreme Court picks: Schumer

Adding to his earlier speech, Democrat Chuck Schumer has now told The Associated Press his party will not allow President Donald Trump to put "a right-winger" on the Supreme Court once it takes power in Congress.
Schumer's suggestion raises the possibility the Democrats may block any presidential nominees for the court if a vacancy becomes available during the remainder of Trump's term.

But he has not said whether the Democrats will look to hold an open vacancy on the court until after the 2028 presidential election, in the same way that Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016.
Schumer said Democrats were "not going to allow any crappy nominees" to be confirmed, including to the lower courts or Trump’s cabinet.
For a Supreme Court nominee to be confirmed and appointed, they must be nominated by the president then vetted in Senate committee hearings.
After that, the Senate debates the election choice and votes to either accept or reject the nomination.
How gerrymandering failed in North Carolina
North Carolina’s first congressional district (NC-1) has now been formally called for Democrat Don Davis.
The result represents another failed Republican attempt at flipping a seat through redistricting.
The state's Republicans redrew the map to favour the party last year.
They moved a significant share of Black voters into a neighbouring district.
They also pushed the hometown of incumbent Davis out of the district. It was explicitly done to get Republican Laurie Buckhout elected to replace him.
I was in the district, in the state’s north-east, on polling day.
Black Democrats I spoke to were angry about this. NC-1 has elected Black Democrats since 1992.
"It’s unfair they’re doing it that way," Rocky Mount voter Addie Johnson said. "It’s cheating, that’s what it comes down to."
"It’s unfair they’re doing it that way," Rocky Mount voter Addie Johnson said.
"It’s cheating, that’s what it comes down to."
But it has not worked.
The AP has now called the race for Davis, who has 50.1 per cent of the vote, compared to Buckhout’s 46.8 per cent, with more than 95 per cent of votes counted.
It was a similar story in North Carolina’s 11th district (NC-11), on the other side of the state. Its boundaries have been redrawn several times in recent years.
NC-11 was held by Republican Chuck Edwards, and was considered a pretty safe red seat.
But Edwards pulled out of the race after an ethics committee found he acted inappropriately towards young female staff (though he disputes the findings).
Democratic farmer Jamie Ager (57.1 per cent) then defeated replacement Republican candidate Jennifer Balkcom (41.3 per cent).
New projections for House seats
There has been some movement in the House of Representatives results, with the Associated Press calling six more seats.
Four of the seats have gone to the Democrats and two to the Republicans.
Here's a breakdown
• Democrat JoAnna Mendoza won the election in Arizona's 6th Congressional District, defeating Republican incumbent Juan Ciscomani
That would bring the total to 251 seats for Democrats and 155 for Republicans in the lower house.
Democrat says '200 investigative letters' are roadmap for likely probes

Further to Chuck Schumer's earlier comments about the Democrats looking into voters' concerns on ''costs, chaos and corruption'' in Congress, Maryland representative Jamie Raskin says he has already laid out a roadmap for investigating Republicans.
Raskin, who was re-elected this week in Maryland's Eighth District House seat with more than 82 per cent of the vote, is the incoming House Judiciary Committee chairman.
He told a Center for American Progress forum today that he’s written 200-plus investigative letters to the Department of Justice and White House during Donald Trump’s second presidency.

''It’s a pretty good trail of crumbs of what we’re going to do,'' he said. ''This is not a game of surprise or gotcha. We’re talking about trying to defend our system of government against authoritarians here.''
''It’s a pretty good trail of crumbs of what we’re going to do,'' he said.
''This is not a game of surprise or gotcha. We’re talking about trying to defend our system of government against authoritarians here.''

He also argued that Trump issuing any pardon related to criminal activity he was involved in personally could constitute an impeachable offence under the US Constitution’s ''high crimes and misdemeanours” standard.
Reporting with AP

Why US stocks are sinking
This is a real post-midterms jitter here. The NASDAQ is falling amid fears that a Democrat-led Congress will curtail AI-driven developments.
And that fear is well-founded. Democrats will believe they have a mandate to pump the brakes on data centres and AI when the new Congress begins.

Democratic Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were some of the first to turn AI into a hot-button political issue, calling for a moratorium on building new data centres back in March.
It's one of the key issues that many Democrats campaigned on.
In fact, one of the candidates who got beaten, Darline Graham, was nicknamed "Data Centre Darline".
She was the sister of the famous Lindsey Graham from South Carolina.
It's one of many reasons she lost a seat Republicans have held for two decades.
And in Texas, data centres became a huge issue; incoming Senator James Talarico aggressively campaigned under a slogan of "Texas is not for sale" and sparred regularly with SpaceX founder Elon Musk.

Data centre-related measures were on the ballot in more than a dozen states—and failed in most—in the clearest indication yet that even if Wall Street is spooked by Democrats taking Congress, Main Street will expect action.
Republicans starting to turn on Hegseth
In the wake of this week's major Republican midterm losses, the political future of Pete Hegseth, Donald Trump's defense secretary remains in limbo.
Some Republican members are starting to turn on Hegseth, as many blame the war on Iran for the party's election defeat.

Kentucky House Republican Thomas Massie posted on social media a short time ago that he believes, "if Trump’s going to replace appointees like Hegseth, he should do it while he can still get the replacements confirmed in the Senate".
However, Massie has promised to impeach Hegseth before he leaves the House at the end of this year.
"My Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress," he said on X. "They’ll have hearings & trials."
"My Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress," he said on X.
"They’ll have hearings & trials."

Massie, who is renowned for his opposition to some Trump policies, lost his re-election bid to represent Kentucky's Fourth District during the party's primary to Ed Gallrein — who went on to win this week's midterm election in that district.
His comments come a day after US Vice-President JD Vance also subtly took aim at the Iran war in his breakdown of the election result.
Hillary Clinton celebrates 'historic gains' by Democratic women
In a post on X, former presidential candidate Hillary Clinton has praised the "historic gains Democratic women made in representation" this election.
She noted that for the first time in history, more than 100 Democratic women will serve in the House and at least 14 will serve as governors.
Clinton added that four states — Georgia, Minnesota, Ohio and Tennessee — elected their first woman governor.
Here are some other historic firsts she highlighted:
• Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms will become the first Black woman to serve as governor anywhere in the US
• New Mexico Democrat Deb Haaland will become the first Native American woman elected governor of a US state
• Democrat Gina Hinojosa will become the first Hispanic woman to hold the gubernatorial seat in Texas
• Minnesota Democrat Peggy Flanagan will become the first Native American woman elected to the Senate

How the midterms state of play looks this morning
Good morning to those still following the US midterm election results closely!
Here's the state of play of what races the Associated Press — which the ABC uses for official calls and projections of US elections — has not yet called:
• Senate: 2 races — Alaska and Mississippi
• Governor: 1 — Alaska
• House of Representatives: 35 races
In Mississippi's Senate race, Democrat Scott Colom has seen his lead of a few dozen votes over Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith grow to 1,724 votes with 96 per cent of ballots counted.

The AP also has not called Alaska's Senate contest between incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, who had a 637-vote lead over Sullivan with an estimated 74 per cent of votes counted.
We're keeping our eyes peeled and will bring you any results as they come through.

Schumer pushes for 'different voices' in Democrat revival
The likely Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer has also hinted at what may come for the party over the coming years.
He said the battle over the party's identity is a distraction and that any governing majority requires a coalition of ''different voices".

''Populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said. ''Unity does not mean blind fealty to a party line. ''Just look at what that’s done to the GOP. ''Unity means linking arms with people you will not agree with on every issue so that you can make progress on the more important areas where you agree.''
''Populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said.
''Unity does not mean blind fealty to a party line.
''Just look at what that’s done to the GOP.
''Unity means linking arms with people you will not agree with on every issue so that you can make progress on the more important areas where you agree.''
Schumer said he believed Democrats flipped so many Senate seats by having ''candidates who fit their states … all united by one simple mission: make the government work for the people".
Key Event
Chuck Schumer hints at how Democrats could cause headaches for Trump
Democrat Chuck Schumer spoke a short time ago and provided some insight into how the new-look Congress could pose political problems for Donald Trump.

The New York representative who is likely to become the Senate majority leader said Congress would work to answer voters’ concerns on ''costs, chaos and corruption'' regardless of whether the president plays along.
''Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’ intransigence, of course not,'' he said at the Center for American Progress.
Schumer also said the Democrats will try to curb Trump’s tariffs, the Iran war, ban federal elected officials from stock trades, and limit consumer costs from data centre expansion.

''If Donald Trump does spend the next year vetoing common sense legislation to lower costs and end corruption, this election … this absolute Republican catastrophe on election night 2026 will look like a good day compared to what will come down on Republicans in the 2028 election.''
Reporting with AP
Key Event
US stocks dive amid predictions of AI pullback after election results
US tech stocks plunged on Thursday, in the wake of this week's lopsided midterm elections.
Analysts pointed to the Democrats dominance at the midterms, saying the market had reacted to the fact data centres were a major election issue around the US.

Many Democrats have insisted state legislatures and politicians in Washington do more to pump the brakes on what critics have described as unbridled development of data centres driven by booming AI companies.

As trading continued into the afternoon, the Dow Jones had wiped off gains made the previous day to be down 1,500 or around 3 per cent, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq plunged more than 5 per cent (that is "correction" territory).
Meanwhile, the S&P 500 shed almost 4 per cent.
Melania hosts Ukrainian, Russian officials
The first lady has hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House as the US ramps up its efforts to secure a deal to end the war.
The event recognised the six-day ceasefire she helped broker in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky.
"We have chosen humanity over war," Melania said. "We must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people."
"We have chosen humanity over war," Melania said.
"We must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people."
The visit marked the first in-person contact between Russian and US officials since Tuesday's midterm elections.
The incoming Democratic majority in Congress is tipped to push for more aid for Ukraine.
College students blame Trump administration for defeat
Republican-supporting American college students have signed an open letter "unequivocally" blaming the Trump administration for the "greatest Republican defeat".
The College Republican Patriot Coalition said "the outcome was no accident" and called for a "revolution" within the party.

"Millions of us young Americans knocked on doors, made calls and cast first-time ballots for a movement that promised affordability, mass deportations, reindustrialisation and an end to foreign wars," the group wrote. "Instead, we received a war on behalf of Israel, stunted deportations and a flailing economy."

"Millions of us young Americans knocked on doors, made calls and cast first-time ballots for a movement that promised affordability, mass deportations, reindustrialisation and an end to foreign wars," the group wrote.
"Instead, we received a war on behalf of Israel, stunted deportations and a flailing economy."
The letter, signed by more than 30 college republicans, said "young Americans are being priced out of their own country".

"A generation told it could build a family and a future has been handed excuse after excuse for an unmitigated failure to deliver results," it said. "We call on President Trump to purge his administration of those who have not and will not deliver on the mandate voters gave him in 2024."

"We call on President Trump to purge his administration of those who have not and will not deliver on the mandate voters gave him in 2024."
The letter said Trump's top priorities must be ending the Iran war and making life affordable for young Americans.
New projections for House seats
The Associated Press, which the ABC uses for official calls and projections of US elections, has made calls in 14 more US House seats in the last hour.
Eight of the seats have gone to the Democrats and six to the Republicans.
That would take the total tally, according to AP, to 247 seats for the Democrats and 153 seats for the Republicans in the lower house.
No movement yet on the Mississippi or Alaska Senate races, but we're keeping our eyes peeled!
Key Event
Trump loyalist Harmeet Dhillon resigns

Dhillon, who was in charge of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, is one of the first high-ranking departures from Donald Trump’s administration to quit following the staggering midterms loss.
Attorney-General Todd Blanche confirmed her resignation.

"Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months," he wrote on X. "She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. "The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."
"Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months," he wrote on X.
"She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor.
"The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."
Dhillon was a Trump ally and oversaw a sweeping overhaul of the civil rights unit.

Cruz calls midterms defeat a 'Watergate-level repudiation'

Republican Texas Senator Ted Cruz, who some readers might remember ran and lost against Donald Trump in the Republican presidential primary in 2016, has blamed a lack of focus on the high cost of living for the drubbing his party received on Tuesday.
In the latest episode of his Verdict podcast, Cruz said Republicans received a "Watergate-level repudiation".

"We've lost the House. We've lost the Senate," he said. "We lost in historically red states like South Carolina and North Carolina and Kansas and Iowa. "Nowhere are the consequences of this election greater than Texas. In the Lone Star state, we lost every single statewide election."
"We've lost the House. We've lost the Senate," he said.
"We lost in historically red states like South Carolina and North Carolina and Kansas and Iowa.
"Nowhere are the consequences of this election greater than Texas. In the Lone Star state, we lost every single statewide election."
Cruz said the result was an "ass-kicking", with voters choosing Democrats.
He said exit polling in Kansas showed the most important issue for voters was the cost of living, followed by corruption and the cost of the Iran war.

"When all the votes were counted, the problem wasn't turn out." "Instead, our voters – Republicans, libertarians, independents – showed up and voted and rejected our candidates, voting Democrats instead."
"When all the votes were counted, the problem wasn't turn out."
"Instead, our voters – Republicans, libertarians, independents – showed up and voted and rejected our candidates, voting Democrats instead."
Cruz was not up for re-election in this year's midterm polls, and will remain in his Senate position until at least 2031.
Key Event
Democrat Katherine Clark runs for Majority House leadership
Massachusetts Democrat Katherine Clark confirms she will run to be the majority leader in the House of Representatives in the next Congress.
In a letter obtained by American broadcaster CBS, Clark asked fellow Democrats for their support.
"Today with pride in what we've achieved and confidence in what we will deliver, I ask for your support," she wrote.
Clark is currently the Democratic House Whip.
If successful, she would be the first woman to become a majority leader in Congress.
"In the words of the great Dolly Parton, it's been a long hard fight, but I see a brand new day a-dawning," she said on Wednesday.
Key Event
Donald Trump hits out over close-run Alaska contest
The US president is keeping an unusually low profile today.
We're yet to see him front the media in person, but he has made one post on social media.
In his Truth Social post, he weighed in on the Alaska Senate count, which as of this moment is yet to be decided.

The race is particularly interesting because it features two Dan Sullivans: Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan and Independent Dan J Sullivan, whom Republicans accuse of being encouraged to run by Democrats to confuse voters.
The situation appears to have frustrated Donald Trump, who wants their vote totals combined and given to Republicans.

"The vote totals for the Fake Dan Sullivan, plus the other “slug” that the Dems put on the Ballot, should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan, and the Election is over - He easily wins. There is no other fair solution! President DJT"
Democrat candidate Mary Peltola is currently leading by a narrow 637-vote margin over Republican Dan Sullivan, and the independent currently has 3,600 votes.
Good morning and welcome to our live blog
We're on deck to bring you the latest developments through this Friday after this week's decisive midterm results.
There's still a decent number of US House races and two key US Senate races still up in the air, and we'll be bringing you the latest from those counts as they progress.
We'll bring you the latest reaction from across the US and around the world, as Republicans face a stunning midterm defeat which will see Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.
Thanks for joining us!
